Establish a joiners, movers, and leavers process to ensure accounts are disabled promptly when users leave or change roles. Review service accounts to confirm they are still in use and remove those that are not.

title: Accounts with 'Password Never Expires' Flag
description: A number of Active Directory user or service accounts have the 'Password Never Expires' flag set, meaning their passwords are never forced to change regardless of the domain password policy. This is particularly concerning for accounts with elevated privileges.
impact: Accounts with passwords that never expire increase the risk that compromised credentials remain valid indefinitely. If a password is exposed through a breach, phishing, or offline cracking and is never rotated, an attacker may retain persistent access to the account without any time-based remediation occurring through normal policy enforcement.
recommendations: Review all accounts with the 'Password Never Expires' flag and assess whether the setting is genuinely necessary. For service accounts, consider migrating to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) which handle password rotation automatically. For user accounts, remove the flag and ensure they are subject to the domain password expiry policy.

title: Domain Password Spraying
description: The domain lacks sufficient controls to prevent or detect low-and-slow password spraying attacks against domain accounts. Password spraying involves attempting a single common password against many accounts to avoid account lockout thresholds.
impact: An attacker may be able to gain valid domain credentials by attempting common or seasonal passwords against domain accounts at a rate that avoids triggering account lockout policies. Once valid credentials are obtained, the attacker has authenticated domain access and can conduct further reconnaissance, lateral movement, or privilege escalation.
recommendations: Implement account lockout policies with appropriate thresholds and observation windows that detect low-and-slow attacks. Deploy Microsoft Entra ID Password Protection or equivalent to prevent the use of common passwords. Monitor for authentication anomalies such as a single source IP authenticating against many different accounts. Enforce multi-factor authentication to reduce the impact of compromised credentials.

title: KRBTGT Account Password Not Recently Rotated
description: The KRBTGT account password has not been rotated recently. The KRBTGT account is used to sign all Kerberos tickets in the domain, and its password hash is used to forge Golden Tickets. If an attacker has previously obtained the KRBTGT hash, they may retain the ability to generate valid Kerberos tickets indefinitely until the password is rotated twice.
impact: If an attacker has previously compromised the domain and obtained the KRBTGT hash, they may be able to continue generating valid Golden Tickets even after remediation efforts, as long as the KRBTGT password has not been rotated twice. This provides persistent covert access to the domain that survives password resets of other accounts and even some reinstallation scenarios.
recommendations: Rotate the KRBTGT account password twice, waiting one Kerberos ticket lifetime (typically 10 hours) between rotations to ensure all tickets signed with the old key expire naturally. Use Microsoft's documented KRBTGT reset script for the first rotation. Establish a process to rotate the KRBTGT password regularly (at least annually, or following any suspected domain compromise).

title: No Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) Policy
description: The organisation does not enforce the use of dedicated Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for administrative tasks. Administrators use the same workstations for general purpose activities such as email and web browsing as they do for performing privileged Active Directory and server administration.
impact: General-purpose workstations used for privileged administration are exposed to the full threat landscape including phishing, malicious web content, and drive-by downloads. If a workstation used by a domain administrator is compromised, an attacker may be able to capture privileged credentials from memory, intercept administrative sessions, or leverage cached privileged tickets to compromise the domain.
recommendations: Implement a Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) strategy where dedicated, hardened workstations are used exclusively for privileged administration tasks. These workstations should be isolated from general internet access, have a minimal software footprint, enforce application whitelisting, and be subject to enhanced monitoring. Implement a tiered administration model to enforce separation of duties across administrative tiers.

title: Privileged Accounts Used for Non-Privileged Tasks
description: Domain administrators and other privileged accounts are being used to perform routine tasks such as browsing the web, reading email, or logging into general workstations. This increases the risk that privileged credentials are exposed to threats that target standard user activity.
impact: Privileged accounts used on workstations or for general tasks are exposed to the full threat landscape targeting those environments, including malware, phishing, and browser exploits. If a privileged account's credentials are captured on a workstation, the attacker immediately gains domain-level access without needing to perform any additional privilege escalation.
recommendations: Enforce a tiered administration model where privileged accounts are only used on dedicated, hardened Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) and are never used for general tasks. Implement controls to prevent privileged accounts from logging into Tier 1 and Tier 2 systems, and educate administrators on the risks of using privileged accounts for non-administrative tasks.

title: Timeroasting – Machine Account Password Hash Extraction
description: Timeroasting exploits the Network Time Protocol synchronisation mechanism used by Active Directory. By sending crafted MS-SNTP requests containing forged timestamps to domain controllers, an unauthenticated attacker can elicit responses signed with the RC4 hash of a machine account's NT password, allowing offline brute-force or dictionary attacks.
impact: An attacker with network access to port 123 (UDP/NTP) may be able to extract RC4-signed NTP responses containing machine account password hashes, then recover machine account credentials offline. Compromised machine accounts may facilitate lateral movement or privilege escalation, particularly where machine accounts hold elevated permissions.
recommendations: Enforce strong, randomly generated passwords for all machine accounts via Managed Service Accounts (gMSA/MSA). Monitor for anomalous NTP requests from non-NTP hosts. Consider deploying honeytoken machine accounts to detect exploitation attempts. Apply available patches addressing MS-SNTP authentication weaknesses.

title: Weak Domain Password Policy
description: The Active Directory domain password policy does not enforce sufficiently strong password requirements. This may include insufficient minimum length, lack of complexity requirements, or password history settings that do not prevent the reuse of recently used passwords.
impact: Users may be permitted to set passwords that are easily guessable or susceptible to dictionary attacks. If an attacker obtains password hashes through techniques such as Kerberoasting, AS-REP Roasting, or DCSync, weak passwords will significantly reduce the time required to crack them offline, increasing the likelihood of domain-wide compromise.
recommendations: Increase the minimum password length to at least 12 characters and enforce password history to prevent reuse of recent passwords. Deploy Microsoft Entra ID Password Protection or a third-party equivalent to block common and previously breached passwords. Consider implementing Fine-Grained Password Policies (FGPPs) to enforce stricter requirements on privileged accounts.

title: Conditional Access Policy Gaps for Privileged Accounts
description:
Ruptura InfoSecurity found several gaps in the current Conditional Access (CA) policies, particularly around high-privileged accounts. The following deficiencies were identified: administrative accounts were not required to authenticate from compliant devices, legacy authentication protocols were not blocked for privileged roles, and sign-in risk policies did not apply to accounts holding Global Administrator, Exchange Administrator, or SharePoint Administrator roles.

Conditional Access policies are the primary control plane for enforcing Zero Trust access requirements in Microsoft Entra ID environments.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Gaps in Conditional Access policy coverage for privileged accounts mean that administrator accounts are reachable from untrusted devices, legacy authentication protocols (which do not support MFA), and high-risk sign-in locations. Compromise of a Global Administrator account grants complete control of the Microsoft 365 tenant and Azure resources.

**Business Impact:** Global Administrator compromise is the highest-impact scenario in a Microsoft 365 environment, enabling attackers to disable security controls, exfiltrate all data, and establish persistent access.
recommendations:
- Implement a dedicated Conditional Access policy for all privileged roles requiring: compliant device, MFA, and blocking of legacy authentication
- Enable Entra ID Protection and configure sign-in risk and user risk Conditional Access policies
- Implement Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for Just-in-Time (JIT) activation of privileged roles
- Enable Conditional Access for Azure management (`microsoft.com/azure`) requiring compliant device and MFA
- Regularly review Conditional Access policy coverage using the Entra ID 'What If' tool

title: Entra ID Legacy Authentication Protocols Not Blocked
description:
Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that legacy authentication protocols (Basic Auth, NTLM, IMAP, POP3, SMTP AUTH) were not blocked via Conditional Access policy. Legacy authentication protocols do not support modern MFA challenges, meaning that any account with a weak or compromised password can be accessed via legacy protocols regardless of MFA being enabled for the account.

Microsoft reports that over 99% of password spray attacks and the majority of credential stuffing attacks targeting Microsoft 365 use legacy authentication protocols to bypass MFA.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Attackers can attempt password spraying and credential stuffing attacks against user accounts via legacy protocols, bypassing MFA requirements entirely. Successful authentication via legacy protocols provides full mailbox access and potentially access to other Microsoft 365 services.

**Business Impact:** Mass account compromise via password spraying is a realistic threat. Compromised mailboxes enable business email compromise (BEC) fraud, data theft, and lateral phishing.
recommendations:
- Create a Conditional Access policy that blocks all legacy authentication: set the Client App condition to `Exchange ActiveSync clients` and `Other clients` with an Effect of `Block`
- Apply this policy to all users, with a short exclusion period for any services that genuinely require legacy authentication
- Identify and migrate any services requiring legacy authentication to OAuth 2.0/modern authentication
- Enable sign-in logs and filter for legacy authentication to identify remaining usage before enforcement

title: Azure Storage Account Access Keys Not Rotated
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that access keys for Azure Storage accounts had never been rotated or had not been rotated within the last 90 days. Storage account access keys provide full administrative access to all data within the storage account, equivalent to account owner permissions. In the event of a key compromise, access persists until the key is manually rotated.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Compromised storage access keys grant the attacker full access to all blobs, queues, tables, and file shares in the storage account. Keys do not expire automatically and cannot be MFA-protected.

**Business Impact:** Leaked access keys (e.g., from source code repositories or configuration files) are actively exploited by threat actors. Regular rotation limits the window of exposure.
recommendations:
- Rotate storage account access keys on a regular basis (minimum 90-day rotation cycle)
- Prefer Azure AD-based authentication (Managed Identities, service principals) over access key authentication where possible
- Store access keys in Azure Key Vault rather than application configuration files
- Enable Azure Storage alerts and Azure Defender for Storage to detect anomalous access patterns
- Use Shared Access Signatures (SAS) with limited permissions and expiry rather than access keys for application-level access

title: Azure Blob Containers Allow Public Access
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified Azure Blob Storage containers configured with public access enabled (either `Blob` or `Container` access level). This allows any unauthenticated user on the internet to read files stored in the container, or in the case of `Container` access, also enumerate all blobs within it. Public blob access should only be enabled when there is an explicit business requirement for unauthenticated access to the stored content.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Public blob access exposes all files in the affected containers to unauthenticated internet access. Sensitive data including PII, business documents, application configuration files, and database backups may be accessible. Container-level access additionally allows blob enumeration.

**Business Impact:** Exposure of sensitive data via public blob containers is a common cause of cloud data breaches. Regulatory breach notification obligations apply if PII is exposed.
recommendations:
- Disable public blob access at the storage account level: set `Allow Blob Anonymous Access` to disabled
- Review all existing containers and remove any unnecessary public access
- Use Shared Access Signatures (SAS) with time-limited, permission-scoped tokens for scenarios requiring temporary external access
- Use Azure CDN or Azure Front Door for public content delivery rather than direct blob public access
- Use Azure Private Endpoints for storage accounts accessed only from internal services

title: Microsoft 365 Phishing-Resistant MFA Not Enforced
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) was not enforced using phishing-resistant methods for all users. Where MFA was enabled, push notification-based methods (Microsoft Authenticator push) were used without number matching or additional context, making them susceptible to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) attacks. Phishing-resistant MFA methods such as FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication are not vulnerable to adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Push-based MFA without number matching is vulnerable to MFA fatigue attacks, where an attacker with valid credentials sends repeated MFA prompts until the user accidentally approves one. AiTM phishing frameworks (Evilginx2, Modlishka) can relay MFA challenges in real time, making all non-phishing-resistant MFA methods bypassable.

**Business Impact:** MFA bypass via fatigue or AiTM attacks is the most common path to Microsoft 365 account compromise. Subsequent BEC fraud costs organisations millions annually.
recommendations:
- Enable number matching and additional context in Microsoft Authenticator push notifications immediately (as an interim measure)
- Migrate all users to phishing-resistant MFA methods: FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication
- Implement Conditional Access requiring phishing-resistant MFA for all privileged accounts as a priority
- Enable Entra ID Identity Protection to detect anomalous sign-in patterns and trigger step-up authentication
- Disable Microsoft Authenticator push without number matching via Authentication Method policies

title: Microsoft Entra ID Privileged Identity Management Not Configured
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that Privileged Identity Management (PIM) was not configured for privileged Entra ID roles. Without PIM, privileged roles are permanently assigned rather than being activated on a just-in-time (JIT) basis. Permanent role assignment means that if a privileged account is compromised, the attacker immediately and continuously has access to all capabilities associated with the role, with no activation approval or time-bounded access constraints.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Permanently assigned privileged roles represent a persistent high-privilege attack surface. Compromised accounts retain full administrative capability indefinitely rather than requiring active role activation. Without PIM, there is no access review, approval workflow, or activation audit trail.

**Business Impact:** Industry best practice (NIST, CIS, Microsoft Security Benchmark) mandates JIT privileged access. Permanent assignment increases breach impact and may fail compliance audits.
recommendations:
- Enable Entra ID PIM for all privileged roles, particularly Global Administrator, Security Administrator, Exchange Administrator, and SharePoint Administrator
- Convert all permanent role assignments to eligible (JIT) assignments
- Configure PIM to require: MFA for activation, manager approval for high-risk roles, justification text, and maximum activation duration of 8 hours
- Enable PIM access reviews on a quarterly basis
- Configure PIM alerts for suspicious activation patterns

title: Database Service Exposed to the Internet
description: A database service such as MySQL, MSSQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or similar is directly accessible from the internet. Database services should not be exposed externally and should only be reachable from the application tier within a private network segment.
impact: An attacker may be able to connect directly to the database service and attempt to authenticate using default, weak, or previously compromised credentials. Successful access would allow the attacker to extract, modify, or delete all data held within the database. Depending on the database platform and configuration, it may also be possible to execute operating system commands or read sensitive files from the host.
recommendations: Immediately restrict the database service to private network access only using firewall rules or network segmentation. Database services should never be directly accessible from the internet. Ensure strong authentication credentials are in use, disable unnecessary features, and ensure the database software is kept up to date.

title: Public Cloud Storage Bucket
description: One or more cloud storage resources such as Amazon S3 buckets, Azure Blob Storage containers, or Google Cloud Storage buckets are configured with public access enabled. This allows any unauthenticated user to list or download the contents of the storage resource without providing any credentials.
impact: An attacker may be able to access all files stored in the publicly accessible storage resource, which depending on its contents could include sensitive documents, application backups, database dumps, user data, private keys, credentials, or source code. In cases where the bucket is also writable, an attacker may be able to upload malicious content, modify existing files, or conduct supply chain attacks if the bucket hosts files consumed by the application.
recommendations: Immediately review and remediate the access control configuration of all cloud storage resources. Disable public access at both the bucket and account level using the cloud provider's public access block settings. Audit the contents of any previously exposed buckets to determine what data may have been accessed. Implement automated monitoring and alerting for public storage bucket configuration changes.

title: RDP Exposed to the Internet
description: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is accessible directly from the internet on one or more systems. RDP is a high-value target for attackers and has a significant history of critical vulnerabilities. Exposing RDP to the internet substantially increases the attack surface.
impact: An attacker may be able to conduct brute force or credential stuffing attacks against RDP to gain interactive access to the affected system. RDP services exposed to the internet are also routinely targeted by ransomware operators and other threat actors seeking initial access. Critical vulnerabilities such as BlueKeep and DejaBlue can result in unauthenticated remote code execution against vulnerable RDP implementations.
recommendations: Remove RDP from internet-facing access immediately. Where remote access is required, mandate the use of a VPN or a jump host before allowing RDP connections. Apply network-level authentication (NLA), restrict access using firewall rules to trusted IP ranges, and implement multi-factor authentication for remote access.

title: SNMP Default Community Strings
description: The SNMP service is accessible and responds to the default community strings 'public' and/or 'private'. SNMP community strings function as passwords and the use of default values allows any attacker to query or modify the device's SNMP-accessible configuration.
impact: An attacker may be able to use the default SNMP community string to retrieve detailed information about the device including its configuration, network topology, running processes, and interface details. Where write access is permitted via the 'private' community string, an attacker may be able to modify device configuration, potentially disrupting services or facilitating further attacks.
recommendations: Change all default SNMP community strings to unique, complex values. Where possible, migrate to SNMPv3 which supports authentication and encryption. Restrict SNMP access using firewall rules to authorised management hosts only, and consider disabling SNMP entirely if it is not required.

title: Administrative Interface Exposed to the Internet
description: An administrative or management interface is accessible directly from the internet. This may include web-based admin panels, network device management interfaces, database administration tools, or similar high-privilege portals not intended for public access.
impact: An attacker may be able to target the administrative interface with credential attacks, exploit known vulnerabilities in the management software, or abuse any unauthenticated functionality. Successful compromise of an administrative interface typically results in full control over the affected system or application, with the potential to affect all users and data managed through it.
recommendations: Restrict access to administrative interfaces to internal networks or VPN connections only, enforced through firewall rules or network segmentation. Implement multi-factor authentication for all administrative access and ensure the interface software is kept up to date.

title: Subdomain Takeover
description: A DNS record for a subdomain of the affected domain points to a cloud service, hosting provider, or third-party platform that is no longer active or claimed by the organisation. An attacker may be able to register the abandoned resource and claim control of the subdomain.
impact: An attacker who claims the abandoned third-party resource may be able to serve content under the affected subdomain, bypassing same-origin policy restrictions and potentially accessing cookies scoped to the parent domain. This could be used to host phishing pages, capture session tokens, bypass CORS controls, or conduct attacks against users who trust the subdomain.
recommendations: Identify and remove all dangling DNS records that point to unclaimed third-party resources. Implement a process for reviewing DNS records when decommissioning services, and regularly audit DNS records to identify subdomain takeover risks. Use subresource integrity and appropriate cookie scoping to limit the impact of subdomain compromise.

title: Telnet Service Accessible
description: A Telnet service was found accessible on the target. Telnet transmits all data, including authentication credentials, in cleartext and does not provide any form of encryption or integrity protection. The protocol is considered obsolete and should not be used in any environment.
impact: An attacker in a position to intercept network traffic may be able to capture credentials and session data transmitted over Telnet in cleartext. If valid credentials are obtained, the attacker may gain unauthorised access to the affected system and any services or data accessible from it.
recommendations: Disable Telnet immediately and replace it with SSH for remote access. Ensure firewall rules restrict access to remote administration services to authorised IP addresses only, and review whether the service is required at all.

title: Expired TLS Certificate
description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has passed its expiry date. Expired certificates cause browser warnings that may lead users to bypass security controls or make it difficult to distinguish legitimate expired certificates from malicious ones.
impact: Browsers and clients will display security warnings when connecting to a server with an expired certificate, which may cause users to distrust the service or bypass certificate validation. An expired certificate also indicates a lapse in certificate lifecycle management, which may affect broader security processes.
recommendations: Renew the TLS certificate immediately and implement a certificate lifecycle management process to ensure certificates are renewed before expiry. Consider using automated certificate management tools such as ACME-based solutions to prevent future lapses.

title: Missing DKIM Record
description: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signing is not configured for the affected domain. DKIM allows receiving mail servers to verify that email messages were authorised by the domain owner and have not been modified in transit.
impact: Without DKIM, email messages sent from the domain cannot be cryptographically verified by receiving servers, making it easier for attackers to successfully spoof the domain in phishing campaigns. The absence of DKIM also reduces the effectiveness of DMARC enforcement, as DMARC relies on either SPF or DKIM alignment to make policy decisions.
recommendations: Configure DKIM signing for all outbound email and publish the corresponding DKIM public key records in DNS. Ensure DKIM keys are of sufficient length (2048 bits minimum) and implement a key rotation process.

title: Missing DNSSEC
description: DNSSEC (Domain Name System Security Extensions) is not enabled for the affected domain. Without DNSSEC, DNS responses cannot be cryptographically verified by resolvers, leaving the domain vulnerable to DNS spoofing and cache poisoning attacks.
impact: Without DNSSEC, an attacker in a position to intercept or influence DNS responses may be able to redirect users to malicious hosts by returning forged DNS records. This could be used to intercept sensitive communications, capture credentials, or serve malicious content to users who believe they are connecting to a legitimate service.
recommendations: Enable DNSSEC for the affected domain and ensure the DS records are published in the parent zone. Regularly monitor DNSSEC signatures to ensure they remain valid and are renewed before expiry.

title: Missing SPF Record
description: No Sender Policy Framework (SPF) record is published for the affected domain. SPF allows domain owners to specify which mail servers are authorised to send email on behalf of the domain, enabling receiving mail servers to reject spoofed messages.
impact: Without an SPF record, an attacker may be able to send email messages that appear to originate from the affected domain without any SPF-based rejection at the receiving server. This makes the domain easier to spoof in phishing and social engineering campaigns, potentially increasing the success rate of attacks targeting the organisation's customers, partners, or staff.
recommendations: Publish an SPF record in DNS that authorises the mail servers legitimately used to send email on behalf of the domain, and use the -all or ~all mechanism to indicate the handling of unauthorised senders. Ensure SPF is implemented alongside DKIM and DMARC for comprehensive email authentication.

title: SMTP User Enumeration via VRFY / EXPN
description: The SMTP server responds to VRFY and/or EXPN commands, allowing unauthenticated users to verify whether specific email addresses or usernames exist on the mail server. These commands are intended for diagnostic purposes and should not be accessible to unauthenticated external users.
impact: An attacker may be able to enumerate valid email addresses and usernames on the mail server by issuing VRFY or EXPN commands. This information can be used to conduct targeted phishing campaigns, perform password spraying attacks against known valid accounts, or identify high-value targets within the organisation.
recommendations: Disable the VRFY and EXPN commands on the mail server by configuring the appropriate settings in the mail server configuration. For Sendmail, use the 'novrfy' and 'noexpn' options; for Postfix, set disable_vrfy_command = yes. Ensure that the RCPT TO command also does not reveal whether recipients exist, to prevent user enumeration via that method.

title: SSH Weak Algorithms Supported
description: The SSH service supports weak or deprecated cryptographic algorithms for key exchange, encryption, or message authentication codes (MACs). This includes algorithms such as diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, arcfour, MD5-based MACs, or other deprecated options.
impact: An attacker in a privileged network position may be able to exploit weak cryptographic algorithms to downgrade or attack the SSH connection. While practical exploitation typically requires significant resources, the presence of weak algorithms increases cryptographic risk and may violate compliance requirements.
recommendations: Configure the SSH server to support only strong cryptographic algorithms. Disable deprecated key exchange algorithms, ciphers, and MACs, and ensure the configuration aligns with current guidance such as the NCSC SSH configuration recommendations or the Mozilla SSH hardening guide.

title: Self-Signed TLS Certificate
description: The server presents a TLS certificate that has been signed by an untrusted or internally generated certificate authority rather than a publicly trusted CA. Clients connecting to the service will receive certificate trust warnings.
impact: Users connecting to the service will receive browser warnings about an untrusted certificate, which may condition them to accept certificate errors and reduce their vigilance against man-in-the-middle attacks. In production environments, self-signed certificates do not provide the same level of identity assurance as certificates issued by a publicly trusted CA.
recommendations: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted certificate authority. For internet-facing services, use a publicly trusted CA. For internal services, establish an internal PKI with appropriate trust distribution, or use a publicly trusted CA where appropriate.

title: Subdomain Enumeration via Information Disclosure
description: Internal or non-public subdomains of the affected domain are discoverable through publicly available information sources such as certificate transparency logs, DNS brute-forcing, search engine indexes, or information disclosed in application responses.
impact: An attacker may be able to discover internal or non-public subdomains that expose additional attack surface, including staging environments, internal APIs, development infrastructure, or administrative portals that are not intended for public access. Information about these subdomains can facilitate targeted reconnaissance and planning of further attacks.
recommendations: Review all subdomains to ensure that internal or non-public services are not accessible from the internet. Use wildcard certificates where possible to reduce subdomain enumeration via certificate transparency logs. Ensure that internal infrastructure hostnames are not disclosed in application responses or error messages.

title: TLS Certificate Hostname Mismatch
description: The common name or subject alternative names on the TLS certificate do not match the hostname used to access the service. Clients will receive certificate validation errors when connecting, and the certificate does not provide the intended identity assurance.
impact: Certificate hostname mismatches prevent clients from cryptographically verifying the identity of the service, which may allow an attacker to perform man-in-the-middle attacks if clients bypass the validation error. The mismatch also indicates a misconfiguration in certificate management processes.
recommendations: Obtain and deploy a TLS certificate that includes the correct hostname in the Subject Alternative Name field. Review certificate issuance and deployment processes to prevent recurrence.

title: Unnecessary Services Exposed
description: The target exposes network services that are not required for its intended purpose and unnecessarily increase the external attack surface. These may include management interfaces, diagnostic services, or legacy protocols that have no business justification for being publicly accessible.
impact: Each unnecessary service exposed to the internet represents an additional attack vector that may be exploited through vulnerabilities in the service software, misconfigurations, or weak authentication. Reducing the attack surface by removing unnecessary services limits the opportunities available to an attacker.
recommendations: Identify and document all services that are required for business operations. Disable or firewall all services that are not required, and implement a regular review process to ensure the attack surface remains minimal. Apply the principle of least exposure to all external-facing systems.

title: Weak DMARC Policy
description: A DMARC record is present for the affected domain, however the policy is set to p=none. This monitoring-only mode does not instruct receiving mail servers to take any action on messages that fail DMARC checks, providing no active protection against domain spoofing.
impact: A DMARC policy of p=none provides no protection against email spoofing, as receiving servers will accept and deliver messages regardless of whether they pass authentication checks. An attacker may still be able to send convincing phishing emails appearing to originate from the affected domain, with DMARC providing no enforcement barrier.
recommendations: Progress the DMARC policy from p=none to p=quarantine, then to p=reject once legitimate mail flows have been confirmed through analysis of DMARC aggregate reports. Ensure SPF and DKIM are correctly configured and aligned before tightening the DMARC policy.

title: Anonymous FTP Access Permitted
description: The FTP service permits anonymous authentication, allowing any user to connect and browse or download files without providing valid credentials. Depending on the server configuration, anonymous users may also be permitted to upload files.
impact: An attacker may be able to access files hosted on the FTP server without requiring credentials, potentially including sensitive data, configuration files, or backups. If write access is permitted, the attacker may also be able to upload malicious content to the server.
recommendations: Disable anonymous FTP access unless it is explicitly required for a business purpose. If anonymous access is necessary, restrict it to a read-only directory containing only non-sensitive public content, and consider migrating to a more secure file transfer protocol such as SFTP or FTPS.

title: Cleartext FTP Service
description: An FTP service is accessible that transmits all data, including authentication credentials and file contents, in cleartext. FTP does not provide any encryption or integrity protection and is considered obsolete for secure file transfer.
impact: An attacker in a position to intercept network traffic may be able to capture FTP credentials and any files transferred during the session. Captured credentials could be used to access the FTP service directly, and depending on the scope of access, may expose sensitive files or provide a foothold on the affected system.
recommendations: Disable cleartext FTP and replace it with a secure alternative such as SFTP or FTPS. If FTP must remain available, ensure it is restricted to specific IP ranges and enforce the use of FTPS (FTP over TLS) to protect credentials and data in transit.

title: DNS Zone Transfer Permitted
description: The DNS server permits zone transfer requests (AXFR/IXFR) from arbitrary sources. Zone transfers are intended for replication between authoritative DNS servers and should not be available to unauthenticated external clients.
impact: An attacker may be able to retrieve the complete DNS zone data for the affected domain, revealing internal hostnames, IP addresses, mail server configurations, and the overall structure of the network. This information can be used to identify further attack targets and plan more effective attacks against the organisation's infrastructure.
recommendations: Restrict DNS zone transfers to authorised secondary DNS servers only, using IP-based access controls or TSIG authentication. Regularly review zone transfer permissions and monitor DNS server logs for unauthorised transfer requests.

title: Dangling DNS Records
description: DNS records were identified that point to IP addresses or services that are no longer under the organisation's control, or that reference resources that no longer exist. These records are commonly left behind when cloud services or hosting arrangements are decommissioned.
impact: Dangling DNS records may allow an attacker to claim the referenced resource and partially or fully control the subdomain associated with the record. Depending on the nature of the record and the trust placed in the subdomain, this could be used for phishing, session hijacking, or bypassing same-origin restrictions.
recommendations: Audit all DNS records and remove or update any that reference resources no longer under the organisation's control. Implement a process to ensure DNS records are cleaned up as part of any service decommissioning activity.

title: Missing DMARC Record
description: No DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) policy is published for the affected domain. DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM to allow domain owners to specify how receiving mail servers should handle messages that fail authentication checks.
impact: Without a DMARC policy, receiving mail servers have no instruction from the domain owner on how to handle email that fails SPF or DKIM checks. This makes the domain significantly more susceptible to spoofing in phishing campaigns, as there is no mechanism to instruct receiving servers to quarantine or reject fraudulent messages purporting to come from the domain.
recommendations: Publish a DMARC record for the affected domain. Begin with a p=none policy to collect reporting data, then progressively move to p=quarantine and p=reject once legitimate mail flows are confirmed. Ensure DMARC reporting addresses are configured to receive aggregate and forensic reports.

title: SMTP Open Relay
description: The mail server is configured as an open relay, accepting and forwarding email messages from unauthenticated external senders to arbitrary destinations. Open relays can be abused to send unsolicited email on behalf of the organisation.
impact: An attacker may be able to use the mail server to send spam, phishing emails, or other malicious messages that appear to originate from the organisation's domain. This could result in the organisation's mail server and domain being blacklisted, causing legitimate email delivery to be disrupted, and could facilitate phishing campaigns that exploit the organisation's trusted reputation.
recommendations: Configure the mail server to restrict relay to authenticated users or specific trusted IP ranges only. Test the configuration after changes using open relay testing tools and monitor outbound mail flows for anomalies.

title: SSH Password Authentication Enabled
description: The SSH service permits password-based authentication in addition to or instead of public key authentication. Password authentication exposes the service to brute force and credential stuffing attacks, particularly when the service is internet-facing.
impact: An attacker may be able to gain unauthorised access to the SSH service by brute-forcing or guessing weak passwords, or by using credentials obtained from other breaches. Successful authentication would provide the attacker with shell access to the affected system with the privileges of the compromised account.
recommendations: Disable password authentication for SSH and enforce public key authentication only. Ensure the SSH configuration sets PasswordAuthentication no and ChallengeResponseAuthentication no. Implement fail2ban or equivalent controls to limit brute force attempts, and restrict SSH access to known IP ranges using firewall rules.

title: TLS 1.0 / TLS 1.1 Enabled
description: The server supports TLS 1.0 and/or TLS 1.1, protocol versions that have been deprecated due to known cryptographic weaknesses including vulnerability to the BEAST and POODLE attacks. Both versions are no longer recommended by standards bodies including the IETF.
impact: An attacker in a privileged network position may be able to exploit weaknesses in TLS 1.0 or 1.1 to downgrade connections and decrypt traffic. While practical exploitation generally requires specific conditions, the use of deprecated protocol versions increases the risk of cryptographic attacks against transmitted data.
recommendations: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on all services and configure the server to support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 only. Ensure clients that require older protocol versions are identified and updated before making configuration changes.

title: Unencrypted HTTP Service
description: The web application or service is accessible over unencrypted HTTP without enforcing a redirect to HTTPS. Data transmitted between the client and server, including credentials and session tokens, is transmitted in cleartext.
impact: An attacker in a privileged network position may be able to intercept and read data transmitted over HTTP, including authentication credentials, session tokens, and sensitive application data. Attackers may also be able to inject malicious content into HTTP responses, modifying application behaviour or serving malicious payloads to users.
recommendations: Enable HTTPS on all services and implement a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS. Configure the Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header to instruct browsers to enforce HTTPS for future connections. Ensure TLS is configured with strong cipher suites and valid certificates.

title: Weak SSH Host Key
description: The SSH server presents a host key that uses a weak algorithm or insufficient key length, such as an RSA key shorter than 2048 bits, a DSA key, or other deprecated key types. Weak host keys provide weaker assurance of the server's identity and may be susceptible to factoring attacks.
impact: An attacker may be able to feasibly factor a short RSA host key or exploit weaknesses in deprecated key algorithms to impersonate the SSH server, facilitating man-in-the-middle attacks against SSH connections. Users connecting to the server may unknowingly connect to an attacker-controlled host without receiving a meaningful warning if their known_hosts entry is for the compromised key.
recommendations: Generate new SSH host keys using strong algorithms and key lengths. Use Ed25519 keys as the preferred option, or RSA keys of at least 3072 bits. Remove support for DSA host keys and other deprecated algorithms. Update client known_hosts files after regenerating host keys to ensure clients validate the new key.

title: Weak TLS Cipher Suites
description: The server supports one or more TLS cipher suites that are considered weak or cryptographically insecure. This includes cipher suites using NULL encryption, export-grade ciphers, RC4, DES, 3DES, or those lacking forward secrecy.
impact: An attacker in a privileged network position may be able to exploit weak cipher suites to decrypt or tamper with encrypted communications between clients and the server. Cipher suites without forward secrecy also allow retroactive decryption of captured traffic if the server's private key is later compromised.
recommendations: Disable weak and deprecated cipher suites and configure the server to support only strong, forward-secret cipher suites such as those using AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 with ECDHE or DHE key exchange. Regularly review cipher suite configuration against current TLS best practice guidance such as that published by NCSC or Mozilla.

title: Default Credentials
description: Default credentials are usernames and passwords supplied by a vendor for initial setup or administration. If these credentials are not changed, they remain valid authentication credentials for the affected system.
impact: An attacker may be able to gain full, unauthorised access to the affected system using publicly known credentials. The extent of access depends on the privileges assigned to the default account, and may include the ability to view or modify configuration settings, access sensitive data, or use the compromised system as a foothold for further attacks against internal infrastructure.
recommendations: Change all default credentials immediately and ensure each system uses unique, strong passwords. Implement a credential rotation policy where appropriate and store credentials securely using a password manager.

title: Cisco Smart Install Protocol Enabled
description: The Cisco Smart Install (SMI) protocol is enabled and accessible on one or more Cisco switches. Smart Install is a plug-and-play configuration and image management feature that operates without authentication. Cisco has issued multiple advisories recommending that Smart Install be disabled when not actively in use.
impact: An attacker with network access to a device running Smart Install can send crafted packets to the Smart Install port (TCP 4786) to retrieve the device's configuration file, modify the configuration, replace the device's IOS image with a malicious version, or execute arbitrary commands on the device. This can result in full compromise of the network device and exposure of credentials, routing information, and network topology data.
recommendations: Disable the Smart Install feature on all Cisco devices using the 'no vstack' command. Apply Cisco's recommended mitigations as documented in their security advisories. Implement access control lists to block traffic to TCP port 4786 from untrusted network segments. Audit all Cisco network devices to confirm Smart Install has been disabled.

title: EternalBlue - MS17-010 (SMB Remote Code Execution)
description: One or more systems within the environment are missing the MS17-010 security patch and are vulnerable to the EternalBlue exploit. This vulnerability in the Windows SMB protocol allows unauthenticated remote code execution by exploiting a buffer overflow in the SMBv1 implementation.
impact: An attacker with network access to an unpatched system may be able to achieve remote code execution as the SYSTEM account without requiring any credentials. EternalBlue was weaponised in the WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware campaigns and remains a reliable vector for unauthenticated compromise. Exploitation of a single vulnerable host within the network can rapidly lead to lateral movement and widespread compromise.
recommendations: Apply the MS17-010 security update to all affected systems immediately. As an interim measure, disable SMBv1 on all systems using Group Policy or PowerShell. Ensure network-level controls prevent direct SMB access between workstations, and segment the network to limit the blast radius of any exploitation.

title: Exposed Kubernetes API Server
description: The Kubernetes API server is accessible from outside the cluster network without sufficient authentication controls. The Kubernetes API is the primary control plane interface and provides complete control over all workloads, secrets, and configuration within the cluster.
impact: An attacker with access to the Kubernetes API server may be able to enumerate cluster resources, access secrets including service account tokens and application credentials, deploy malicious workloads, escape to the underlying node operating system using privileged containers, and pivot to any service or system reachable from within the cluster.
recommendations: Restrict access to the Kubernetes API server to authorised networks and management hosts using firewall rules and Kubernetes API server admission controls. Enable and enforce RBAC policies to limit what authenticated users can do. Disable anonymous authentication, rotate service account tokens regularly, and consider deploying network policies to restrict pod-to-pod communication.

title: IPMI / iDRAC / BMC Accessible Without Authentication
description: Out-of-band management interfaces including IPMI, iDRAC, iLO, or similar BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) interfaces are accessible on the network and are either using default credentials or are accessible without authentication. These interfaces provide hardware-level control over the physical server.
impact: An attacker who gains access to an IPMI or BMC interface can exercise complete control over the physical host, including the ability to mount virtual media, read and write to system memory, control power, view the screen, and in some cases extract credentials. Compromising the BMC provides a persistent access channel that is independent of the operating system and survives reimaging.
recommendations: Isolate IPMI and BMC interfaces on a dedicated, highly restricted management network segment with no internet connectivity and strict access controls. Change all default credentials immediately, enable the most recent firmware to patch known vulnerabilities including the IPMI cipher 0 authentication bypass, and disable IPMI if it is not required.

title: Jenkins - Unauthenticated Access or Script Console Exposed
description: The Jenkins CI/CD server allows unauthenticated access to the dashboard or has the Groovy Script Console accessible to low-privileged users. The Script Console provides unrestricted code execution on the Jenkins server and any connected build agents.
impact: An attacker with access to the Jenkins Script Console can execute arbitrary Groovy code on the Jenkins server, which typically results in full remote code execution with the privileges of the Jenkins process. This provides access to all secrets, credentials, and source code managed by Jenkins, as well as potential lateral movement to any system that the Jenkins service account can reach.
recommendations: Enable authentication on the Jenkins instance and restrict access to the Script Console to administrators only. Audit the Jenkins configuration for anonymous access settings and review all user permissions. Store all credentials in the Jenkins Credentials Store rather than in pipeline configuration, and restrict the permissions of the Jenkins service account on the host system.

title: Network Device Default Credentials
description: One or more network devices including switches, routers, or firewalls are accessible using default vendor-supplied credentials. These credentials are publicly documented and allow any attacker with network access to fully authenticate to the management interface.
impact: An attacker may be able to gain full administrative control of the affected network device using the default credentials. This could allow the attacker to modify routing tables, capture network traffic, disable security controls, create unauthorised access paths, or use the device as a pivot point for further attacks against the network.
recommendations: Change all default credentials on all network devices to unique, strong passwords immediately. Implement centralised authentication using RADIUS or TACACS+ where supported, and restrict management access to network devices to a dedicated management network or IP range. Audit all network devices for default credential usage as part of regular security reviews.

title: Unauthenticated Docker API
description: The Docker daemon's remote API is exposed on the network without authentication. The Docker API provides complete control over all container operations on the host and, when accessible without authentication, allows any user who can reach the port to fully control the Docker environment.
impact: An attacker who can reach the Docker API may be able to list and access existing containers and their data, create new containers with host mounts to read or write arbitrary files on the host filesystem, escape to the underlying host operating system, or execute commands within existing containers. A privileged container can be used to gain root access to the host system.
recommendations: Disable the Docker remote API if it is not required for remote management. If the API must be exposed, enable TLS authentication using client certificates to restrict access. Bind the API socket to localhost or a specific management interface, and implement firewall rules to restrict access to the Docker port to authorised management hosts only.

title: Unauthenticated Memcached Instance
description: A Memcached instance is accessible on the network without authentication. Memcached does not implement authentication by default and stores all data in plaintext in memory. An attacker who can reach the service can read and modify all cached data.
impact: An attacker may be able to retrieve all data held in the Memcached cache, which depending on the application may include session tokens, user data, authentication credentials, or other sensitive cached content. An attacker may also be able to poison cached data, causing the application to serve modified content to users. Additionally, internet-accessible Memcached instances can be abused for UDP reflection amplification attacks with amplification factors exceeding 50,000x.
recommendations: Restrict Memcached to listen on the loopback interface or bind it to a specific application-tier interface, ensuring it is never accessible from untrusted networks. Implement firewall rules to restrict access to the Memcached port to the application servers that require it. Disable UDP support unless it is required, as it is the primary vector for amplification attacks.

title: Unauthenticated MongoDB Instance
description: A MongoDB database instance is accessible on the network without authentication. Older versions of MongoDB did not enforce authentication by default, and misconfigured instances may bind to all interfaces and accept connections from any host without requiring credentials.
impact: An attacker with network access to the MongoDB instance may be able to read, modify, or delete all data within all databases hosted on the instance. This could expose sensitive application data, user records, credentials, or business-critical information. An attacker may also be able to insert or modify records, corrupting application data or escalating privileges within the application.
recommendations: Enable MongoDB authentication immediately and ensure all database users have strong, unique credentials with the minimum privileges required. Bind MongoDB to a specific application-tier interface rather than all interfaces, and implement firewall rules to restrict access to the MongoDB port to authorised hosts only. Ensure the MongoDB version in use is current and supported.

title: Unauthenticated Redis Instance
description: A Redis instance is accessible on the network without authentication required. Redis is an in-memory data store that should always require authentication and should not be exposed beyond a trusted application tier.
impact: An attacker with access to the Redis instance can read and modify all data stored in memory, which may include session tokens, cached user data, application configuration, or sensitive business data. In certain configurations, it may also be possible to write files to disk via the Redis CONFIG command or achieve remote code execution by writing to cron or SSH authorized_keys files.
recommendations: Enable Redis authentication by configuring the requirepass directive and using a strong, unique password. Bind Redis to a specific interface or loopback address rather than all interfaces. Implement firewall rules to restrict access to the Redis port to the application servers that require it. Upgrade to a version of Redis that supports ACL-based authentication.

title: VNC Service Exposed with Weak or No Authentication
description: A Virtual Network Computing (VNC) service is accessible on the network and is either configured with no authentication, uses a weak or default password, or uses the deprecated VNC authentication scheme which is vulnerable to offline brute force attacks due to its use of a weak challenge-response mechanism.
impact: An attacker who can reach the VNC service may be able to gain full graphical access to the desktop of the affected system without valid credentials. This provides complete interactive control of the system equivalent to physical access, allowing the attacker to execute commands, install malware, access sensitive data, and pivot to other systems.
recommendations: Immediately disable VNC if it is not required. If remote graphical access is needed, replace VNC with a more secure alternative. Where VNC must remain in use, enforce strong password authentication, restrict access using firewall rules to authorised management hosts only, and configure VNC to tunnel over SSH or VPN. Ensure VNC is never directly accessible from untrusted networks.

title: Anonymous SMB Share Access
description: One or more SMB file shares are accessible to unauthenticated or null session users. SMB shares should require authentication before granting access to any content.
impact: An attacker without domain credentials may be able to browse and download files from accessible SMB shares, potentially including sensitive documents, configuration files, scripts, or credentials. Depending on the content of the shares, this could provide an attacker with information to conduct further attacks or directly expose sensitive business data.
recommendations: Disable null session access to SMB shares by configuring the RestrictNullSessAccess registry key. Review all share permissions and ensure that at minimum authenticated domain users are required to access any share. Remove shares that are not actively required and apply the principle of least privilege to share permissions.

title: Cleartext Credentials Stored in Files
description: Plaintext credentials were discovered stored in files accessible within the environment. This may include configuration files, scripts, batch files, text documents, or other file formats containing usernames and passwords in cleartext.
impact: An attacker who gains access to the filesystem or file shares where the credentials are stored may be able to retrieve plaintext credentials without needing to crack any hash. Depending on the nature of the credentials found, this could provide access to databases, applications, domain accounts, or other critical systems.
recommendations: Remove cleartext credentials from all files and replace them with secure alternatives such as secrets management solutions (e.g. HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) or Windows Credential Manager. Audit file systems and shares for credentials using automated scanning tools and implement data loss prevention controls to detect future credential exposure.

title: DLL Hijacking Opportunity
description: One or more applications or services are susceptible to DLL hijacking, where a malicious DLL can be placed in a directory that the application searches before the legitimate DLL location. This is commonly caused by applications loading DLLs from the current working directory or from non-standard paths writable by low-privileged users.
impact: An attacker who can write to a directory searched by a vulnerable application may be able to place a malicious DLL that is loaded when the application starts. If the application runs with elevated privileges, the malicious code will execute at those elevated privileges, resulting in privilege escalation on the affected host.
recommendations: Identify applications susceptible to DLL hijacking using tools such as Procmon and update them or their configurations to use fully qualified DLL paths. Audit the permissions of application directories and ensure low-privileged users cannot write to locations in the DLL search path. Apply application manifests to restrict DLL loading where supported.

title: End-of-Life Operating System in Use
description: One or more systems within the environment are running operating system versions that have reached end-of-life and no longer receive security updates from the vendor. This includes versions such as Windows Server 2008, Windows 7, or equivalent end-of-life Linux distributions.
impact: Systems running end-of-life operating systems will not receive patches for newly discovered vulnerabilities, meaning any vulnerability identified after the end-of-support date remains permanently unpatched. Attackers routinely target end-of-life systems as they are guaranteed to remain vulnerable to known exploits.
recommendations: Plan and execute the migration of end-of-life systems to supported operating system versions as a priority. Where immediate migration is not possible, implement compensating controls such as network segmentation, additional monitoring, application whitelisting, and restriction of inbound connectivity to the affected systems.

title: Hypervisor Management Interface Exposed
description: A hypervisor management interface such as VMware vCenter, ESXi host management, or Hyper-V Manager is accessible from general network segments without network-level access controls restricting access to authorised management hosts.
impact: An attacker who gains access to the hypervisor management interface may be able to view, clone, modify, or delete all virtual machines running on the hypervisor. This provides a means to extract virtual machine disk images containing sensitive data and credentials, deploy malicious virtual machines, or disrupt all services hosted on the affected hypervisor.
recommendations: Restrict access to hypervisor management interfaces to a dedicated management network segment accessible only from Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs). Implement strong authentication including MFA for hypervisor management access and ensure all management interfaces are running fully patched software.

title: IPv6 SLAAC/DHCPv6 Misconfiguration
description: IPv6 is enabled on network interfaces throughout the environment but is not being actively managed. Hosts that do not require IPv6 are responding to Router Advertisement (RA) and DHCPv6 messages, making them susceptible to rogue RA and MITM6 attacks that redirect IPv6 and potentially IPv4 traffic through an attacker-controlled host.
impact: An attacker on the local network segment may be able to send rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements to redirect traffic from victim hosts through an attacker-controlled machine, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks. Combined with WPAD abuse or NTLM relay attacks, this can lead to credential capture and lateral movement across the environment.
recommendations: If IPv6 is not required, disable it via Group Policy using the DisabledComponents registry key. If IPv6 is in use, deploy Router Advertisement Guard (RA Guard) on network switches to prevent rogue RA messages. Implement DHCPv6 snooping and deploy monitoring to detect anomalous IPv6 traffic patterns.

title: Insecure Scheduled Task Permissions
description: One or more Windows scheduled tasks are configured to run with elevated privileges, and the task executable, script, or working directory can be modified by low-privileged users. This allows an attacker to substitute or modify the content that is executed when the task runs.
impact: An attacker with access to a low-privileged account may be able to modify the script or binary executed by the scheduled task and wait for the task to run, at which point their malicious code will execute with the task's configured privileges. If the task runs as SYSTEM or a domain account with administrative rights, this results in privilege escalation.
recommendations: Audit all scheduled tasks and ensure that the executables and scripts they reference are owned by and only writable by administrators. Review task configurations to ensure they use the minimum privilege level necessary and remove any tasks that are no longer required.

title: Local Administrator Password Reuse (LAPS Not Deployed)
description: Microsoft Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) is not deployed within the environment, and the built-in local administrator account uses the same password across multiple or all domain-joined systems. This allows a hash or credential captured from one system to be reused across the entire estate.
impact: An attacker who extracts the local administrator NTLM hash from one compromised system may be able to authenticate to all other systems sharing that password using pass-the-hash techniques. This enables rapid, automated lateral movement across the entire environment from a single point of compromise, significantly increasing the blast radius of any initial access.
recommendations: Deploy Microsoft LAPS or a third-party equivalent to ensure that each domain-joined system has a unique, automatically rotated local administrator password. Disable or rename the built-in Administrator account where possible, and monitor for lateral movement patterns using Windows event logs and EDR telemetry.

title: Missing Critical Security Patches
description: One or more systems within the environment have not received critical or important security patches within an acceptable timeframe. Unpatched vulnerabilities, particularly those with publicly available exploit code, represent a significant and measurable risk.
impact: Systems missing critical security patches may be exploited by attackers using publicly available tools and exploit code. The specific impact depends on the nature of the unpatched vulnerabilities but could include remote code execution, privilege escalation, or denial of service. Unpatched internet-facing systems are routinely scanned and exploited by automated attack tools.
recommendations: Implement a patch management process that ensures critical security patches are applied within a defined timescale, typically 14 days for critical vulnerabilities and 30 days for high severity. Use vulnerability scanning to maintain visibility of patch status across the environment and prioritise patching based on exploitability and exposure.

title: NFS Shares World-Readable
description: Network File System (NFS) shares are exported with overly permissive access controls, allowing any host on the network or a broad network range to mount and read the share without requiring authentication. NFS relies on IP-based access controls and does not enforce user-level authentication.
impact: An attacker with network access to the NFS server may be able to mount the exposed shares and read all files contained within them. Depending on the content of the shares, this could expose sensitive data, credentials, private keys, application source code, or configuration files. Where write access is permitted, an attacker may also be able to modify or plant files on the share.
recommendations: Restrict NFS exports to specific trusted host IP addresses or subnets rather than using wildcard exports. Apply the ro option to shares that do not require write access, and enable root_squash on all exports to prevent remote root users from having root-level access to the share. Consider migrating to an authenticated file sharing protocol such as SMB with Kerberos authentication.

title: SMBv1 Protocol Enabled
description: The SMBv1 protocol is enabled on one or more systems within the environment. SMBv1 is a legacy protocol that has been deprecated by Microsoft and contains numerous well-documented vulnerabilities. Its presence substantially increases the attack surface beyond the specific risk of any individual CVE.
impact: Systems with SMBv1 enabled are susceptible to a range of exploitation techniques including NTLM relay over SMBv1, exploitation of known critical vulnerabilities such as MS17-010 (EternalBlue), and various information disclosure weaknesses inherent in the protocol. SMBv1 also lacks the encryption and integrity protections present in later protocol versions, making it susceptible to traffic interception.
recommendations: Disable SMBv1 on all systems using Group Policy (Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false) and remove the SMBv1 Windows feature. Audit the environment to identify any legacy systems or applications that may depend on SMBv1 and plan their migration or replacement. Monitor for SMBv1 traffic as an indicator of legacy system presence.

title: Sensitive Data on Accessible Network Shares
description: Network file shares accessible to standard domain users contain sensitive data including credentials, private keys, configuration files, or confidential business information that should be subject to stricter access controls.
impact: An attacker with standard domain access may be able to access sensitive files on network shares, potentially including stored credentials, SSH or API keys, database connection strings, or confidential business documents. This information can directly facilitate further privilege escalation or provide an attacker with access to additional systems and services.
recommendations: Audit all network share permissions and remove access to sensitive directories from accounts that do not require it. Implement data classification and apply access controls based on data sensitivity. Audit share contents to identify and relocate or remove any credentials or sensitive configuration data stored on shared drives.

title: TFTP Server Accessible
description: A Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server is accessible on the network. TFTP provides no authentication mechanism and transmits all data in cleartext. It is commonly used for transferring configuration files and firmware to network devices but should be restricted to dedicated management networks.
impact: An attacker with network access to the TFTP server may be able to download files stored on it, which commonly include network device configuration files containing credentials, SNMP community strings, and network topology information. Where write access is permitted, an attacker may be able to upload modified configuration files or malicious firmware to be loaded by network devices.
recommendations: Restrict TFTP access using firewall rules to authorised management hosts and network devices only. Where possible, isolate the TFTP server on a dedicated management network segment. Audit the files available on the TFTP server and remove any that contain credentials or sensitive information. Consider whether TFTP can be replaced with a more secure file transfer method for network device management.

title: Unauthenticated Elasticsearch Instance
description: An Elasticsearch instance is accessible without authentication, allowing any user who can reach the service to query, modify, or delete all data stored within the cluster. Elasticsearch does not enforce authentication by default in older versions.
impact: An attacker with access to the Elasticsearch instance may be able to retrieve all indexed data, which could include sensitive documents, user information, application logs, or other business data depending on what the application is indexing. An attacker may also be able to modify or delete data, causing data loss or integrity violations.
recommendations: Enable X-Pack Security or the built-in security features available in Elasticsearch 8.x and above to enforce authentication and authorisation. Restrict network access to the Elasticsearch API using firewall rules, and ensure the service is not exposed beyond the application tier. Audit indexed data to identify and remove any sensitive information that should not be stored in Elasticsearch.

title: Unquoted Service Path
description: One or more Windows services are configured with executable paths that contain spaces and are not enclosed in quotation marks. When Windows attempts to resolve the path, it may try to execute a binary in a parent directory if an attacker can place a file at an intermediate path location.
impact: An attacker with write access to a directory in the path resolution chain may be able to place a malicious executable that is executed when the service starts. Depending on the service account used, this could result in privilege escalation to SYSTEM or to the privileges of the configured service account, leading to full compromise of the affected host.
recommendations: Identify all services with unquoted binary paths using automated auditing tools and update the service configurations to enclose paths in quotation marks. Audit the permissions of parent directories in affected paths to ensure low-privileged users cannot write to them.

title: Weak Windows Service Permissions
description: One or more Windows services have been configured with excessive permissions, allowing low-privileged users to modify the service binary path, change the service configuration, or directly modify the executable file referenced by the service.
impact: An attacker with access to a low-privileged account may be able to modify the service configuration to point to a malicious executable, or directly replace the service binary. When the service is restarted or the system reboots, the malicious code will execute with the privileges of the service account, which may be SYSTEM or a highly privileged domain account.
recommendations: Audit service permissions using tools such as Accesschk and correct any that grant modification rights to non-administrative users. Ensure that service binaries and their parent directories are owned by and only writable by administrator-level accounts. Review service account privileges and apply the principle of least privilege.

title: WinRM Accessible with Password-Based Authentication
description: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is accessible on one or more systems and permits password-based authentication. WinRM provides remote PowerShell execution and administrative access equivalent to interactive login, and its exposure across the network significantly increases lateral movement opportunities.
impact: An attacker with valid credentials for an account with WinRM access may be able to establish remote PowerShell sessions and execute arbitrary commands on the affected system with the privileges of the authenticated account. WinRM is also a common target for pass-the-hash attacks, as NTLM authentication is accepted by default, enabling attackers to authenticate using captured password hashes without knowing the plaintext password.
recommendations: Restrict WinRM access using Windows Defender Firewall rules to authorised management hosts and jump servers only. Enforce Kerberos authentication rather than NTLM for WinRM where possible. Implement PowerShell language mode restrictions and logging to limit and record what commands can be executed via remote sessions. Consider whether WinRM needs to be enabled on workstations and disable it where not required.

title: UPnP Enabled on Network Devices
description: Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) is enabled on one or more network devices. UPnP allows devices to automatically discover and interact with each other on the local network and can be abused by malicious software or an attacker on the network to modify firewall rules and port mappings without authentication.
impact: An attacker or malware on the internal network may be able to abuse UPnP to create port forwarding rules on the network gateway, exposing internal services to the internet. This can be used to establish persistent external access to compromised internal systems or to expose internal services that are not intended to be publicly accessible.
recommendations: Disable UPnP on all network devices, particularly routers, firewalls, and switches, unless it is specifically required for a documented business purpose. Most enterprise environments have no legitimate need for UPnP. Regularly audit network device configurations to ensure UPnP does not become re-enabled during firmware updates.

title: Cleartext Protocol Use for Internal Services
description: Internal services and applications are communicating over cleartext protocols such as HTTP, FTP, or Telnet rather than their encrypted equivalents. This includes communication between application tiers as well as between management tools and the systems they manage.
impact: An attacker in a position to intercept internal network traffic, for example through ARP spoofing, rogue device placement, or compromise of a network device, may be able to capture credentials, session tokens, or sensitive data transmitted in cleartext between internal systems. Internal network traffic is often trusted and less monitored, making it a valuable target.
recommendations: Migrate all internal services to encrypted protocols. Replace HTTP with HTTPS, FTP with SFTP or FTPS, and Telnet with SSH. Implement TLS for all inter-service communication and use TLS mutual authentication where appropriate. Apply the principle that encryption should be enforced for all communications, even within internal networks.

title: Insufficient Transport Layer Security on Internal Services
description: Internal services including intranet portals, internal APIs, monitoring dashboards, and management interfaces communicate over HTTP rather than HTTPS, or use TLS configurations with significantly weaker settings than internet-facing services. Internal traffic is often assumed to be safe and exempt from encryption requirements.
impact: An attacker who has gained an initial foothold within the internal network, or who is positioned to intercept internal traffic through ARP spoofing or rogue device placement, may be able to capture credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data transmitted over unencrypted internal connections. The assumption that internal traffic is trusted and does not require encryption significantly increases the value of any network-level foothold.
recommendations: Implement HTTPS on all internal services, including intranet portals, internal APIs, and administrative interfaces. Apply consistent TLS configuration standards to internal services as are applied to internet-facing services. Consider implementing mutual TLS (mTLS) for service-to-service communication to provide both encryption and mutual authentication.
