description: Session cookie flags are security attributes that control how browsers handle session cookies. Missing or incorrectly configured cookie flags can allow session cookies to be accessed or transmitted in ways that increase the risk of session compromise.
impact: Depending on which flags are absent, session cookies may be transmitted over unencrypted connections, accessed by client-side scripts, or submitted in cross-site requests. If a session token is exposed as a result, an attacker could use it to impersonate the affected user and access any functionality or data available to that account.
recommendations: Configure session cookies with appropriate security attributes, including Secure to restrict transmission over HTTPS, HttpOnly to prevent client-side scripts from accessing cookies, and SameSite to reduce cross-site request risks. Regularly review session cookie configuration across the application.

title: Missing Subresource Integrity (SRI)
description: The application loads JavaScript or CSS resources from third-party CDNs without implementing Subresource Integrity (SRI) checks. Without SRI, any compromise of the third-party CDN or the delivery infrastructure could result in malicious content being served to the application's users.
impact: If a third-party CDN from which the application loads resources is compromised, an attacker could replace legitimate scripts or stylesheets with malicious versions. Without SRI validation, the browser will execute the modified content with full trust, potentially allowing the attacker to steal credentials, capture sensitive data, or execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the application.
recommendations: Add integrity attributes containing cryptographic hashes to all script and link elements that reference third-party resources. Generate SRI hashes using the openssl or SRI hash generator tools and include them alongside the crossorigin='anonymous' attribute. Regularly verify that the hashes match the currently deployed versions of third-party resources.

title: Open Redirect
description: The application accepts user-controlled input that determines the destination of a redirect without validating that the target URL is on a trusted domain. An attacker can craft a URL hosted on the legitimate application domain that redirects users to an arbitrary external site.
impact: An attacker may be able to craft links that appear to originate from the legitimate application domain but redirect victims to attacker-controlled sites. This can be used to increase the credibility of phishing attacks, bypass referrer-based controls on external sites, or steal OAuth tokens that are passed as URL parameters if the redirect is triggered mid-flow.
recommendations: Validate redirect destinations against an allow-list of trusted domains or relative URL patterns. Avoid using user-controlled input to determine redirect targets. If external redirects are necessary, display an interstitial warning page informing users they are being redirected to a third-party site.

title: Referrer Header Information Leakage
description: The application does not set an appropriate Referrer-Policy header, causing the browser to include the full URL of the current page in the Referer header when users navigate to external links or when the page loads third-party resources. This can expose sensitive URL parameters, session tokens, or internal path information to external parties.
impact: Sensitive information contained in page URLs, such as password reset tokens, session identifiers, search queries, or internal path names, may be disclosed to third-party services via the Referer header. This information could be accessed by third-party analytics providers, advertisers, or CDN operators whose resources are loaded by the page, and could also be captured by an attacker who controls one of those services.
recommendations: Set a Referrer-Policy HTTP header on all responses to restrict the information included in the Referer header when navigating to or loading resources from external origins. A policy of strict-origin-when-cross-origin is recommended as a sensible default that preserves referrer information for same-origin requests while limiting cross-origin leakage.

title: User Enumeration
description: User enumeration occurs when an application reveals whether a username or account exists through differences in application responses, such as error messages, response codes, or response timing.
impact: An attacker may be able to compile a list of valid usernames or email addresses registered within the application. This information can be used to conduct more targeted brute force or credential stuffing attacks against confirmed accounts, reducing the effort required to achieve an unauthorised authentication.
recommendations: Avoid revealing whether an account exists through application responses. Use consistent error messages and response behaviour for valid and invalid users, and implement rate limiting and monitoring to detect attempts to enumerate accounts.

title: Verbose Error Messages
description: The application returns detailed error messages that expose internal implementation details, stack traces, database query structures, file paths, or framework and library version information. Verbose error messages are often triggered by invalid input or unexpected application states.
impact: An attacker may be able to gain information about the application's underlying technology stack, internal file structure, database schema, or application logic through verbose error messages. This information can be used to identify specific vulnerabilities, craft more targeted attacks, or infer the presence of additional attack surfaces.
recommendations: Configure the application to return generic error messages to users and log detailed error information securely on the server side. Ensure that exception handling does not expose stack traces or internal details in HTTP responses. Implement a global error handler to intercept unhandled exceptions and return safe, non-informative error pages.

title: Weak Content Security Policy
description: A weak Content Security Policy (CSP) occurs when an application implements a CSP that does not sufficiently restrict the sources or execution of browser content. This may reduce the effectiveness of CSP as a security control.
impact: If another client-side vulnerability such as cross-site scripting is present, a weak Content Security Policy may fail to prevent or limit the execution of malicious scripts within a user's browser. This reduces the defence-in-depth protection provided by the CSP and may increase the impact of any client-side vulnerabilities that exist within the application.
recommendations: Review and strengthen the Content Security Policy to restrict resource loading and script execution to trusted sources only. Remove unsafe directives such as unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval where possible, avoid overly broad wildcard sources, and regularly review CSP rules as the application changes.

title: Wordpress XMLRPC Available
description: WordPress XML-RPC is a remote procedure call interface that allows external applications to interact with a WordPress installation. If enabled and not required, it may expose additional functionality that can be targeted by attackers.
impact: An attacker may be able to abuse the XML-RPC interface to conduct credential brute force attacks at an amplified rate using the system.multicall method, enumerate valid user accounts, or trigger interactions with the WordPress installation. If valid credentials are obtained through this interface, the attacker may be able to gain access to the WordPress administrative panel.
recommendations: Disable XML-RPC functionality if it is not required. If XML-RPC is necessary, restrict access where possible, monitor usage, and implement appropriate authentication protections and rate limiting controls.

title: phpinfo() or Server Status Page Accessible
description: A PHP information page (phpinfo()) or web server status page (server-status, server-info) is publicly accessible. These pages expose detailed information about the server environment including PHP configuration, installed extensions, environment variables, loaded modules, and active connections.
impact: An attacker may be able to retrieve detailed information about the server's configuration and environment from these pages, including PHP version and configuration directives, server software versions, file paths, environment variables that may contain credentials, and information about current active requests. This information facilitates targeted attack planning and may directly expose sensitive configuration data.
recommendations: Remove or restrict access to phpinfo() pages from production environments. Disable the server-status and server-info modules in the web server configuration, or restrict them to localhost or specific management IP addresses. Audit the application for any diagnostic pages that expose configuration information and ensure they are not accessible in production.

title: CRLF Injection / HTTP Response Splitting
description: The application incorporates user-supplied input into HTTP response headers without stripping carriage return (\r) and line feed (\n) characters. By injecting CRLF sequences, an attacker can terminate the current header and inject additional headers or body content into the HTTP response.
impact: An attacker may be able to inject arbitrary HTTP headers into the response, set malicious cookies, perform cross-site scripting via injected content, poison web caches to serve malicious responses to other users, or conduct header injection attacks against users of the application. In some configurations, complete response body content can be controlled by the attacker.
recommendations: Strip or encode carriage return and line feed characters from all user-supplied input before including it in HTTP response headers. Use framework-provided methods for setting headers and redirects rather than constructing them manually from user input. Implement a Content Security Policy to limit the impact of any injected content.

title: CSV / Formula Injection
description: The application allows user-supplied data to be exported in CSV or spreadsheet formats without sanitising values that begin with characters interpreted as formula initiators by spreadsheet applications, such as =, +, -, or @. When opened in applications like Microsoft Excel or LibreOffice Calc, these values are executed as formulae.
impact: An attacker may be able to inject spreadsheet formulae into exported data that execute when a recipient opens the file in a spreadsheet application. This could be used to exfiltrate data from the victim's machine via outbound HTTP requests using the WEBSERVICE or similar formula functions, execute dynamic data exchange (DDE) payloads, or in older versions of spreadsheet software, potentially execute arbitrary commands on the recipient's machine.
recommendations: Sanitise all user-supplied data before including it in CSV or spreadsheet exports by prefixing values that begin with =, +, -, @, or tab characters with a single quote or by wrapping them in double quotes and stripping formula characters. Implement server-side validation to reject or sanitise potentially dangerous values at the point of input.

title: Cleartext Password Transmission
description: The application transmits user passwords or other credentials over an unencrypted HTTP connection rather than HTTPS. This may occur on the login form, password change flow, or API authentication endpoints.
impact: An attacker in a position to intercept network traffic may be able to capture credentials transmitted in cleartext over HTTP. This could include user passwords that may be reused across multiple services, allowing the attacker to access the affected account and potentially additional accounts through credential reuse.
recommendations: Enforce HTTPS on all pages and endpoints that handle credentials. Implement HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) to instruct browsers to never connect over plain HTTP. Ensure the login form itself is served over HTTPS so that the browser displays the connection as secure before the user enters their credentials.

title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Misconfiguration
description: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration occurs when an application implements overly permissive or insecure CORS policies, allowing unauthorised web origins to interact with protected resources.
impact: An attacker may be able to make credentialled cross-origin requests to the application from a malicious website and read the resulting responses. If the affected endpoints expose sensitive data such as personal information, API keys, or session-related content, this data could be silently exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled server when a victim visits the malicious page.
recommendations: Restrict CORS policies to only allow trusted origins and avoid using wildcard (*) origins for sensitive resources. Do not allow credentials to be sent with untrusted origins and regularly review CORS configurations to ensure they align with the application's requirements.

title: DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when client-side JavaScript processes user-supplied input and inserts it into the Document Object Model (DOM) in an unsafe manner. An attacker can supply crafted input that is executed within the context of the victim's browser.
impact: An attacker may be able to craft a malicious URL that, when visited by a victim, causes JavaScript to execute within the context of their browser session. This could be used to steal session cookies, capture keystrokes, redirect the user to a malicious site, or perform actions within the application on behalf of the victim.
recommendations: Avoid inserting untrusted data into the DOM using unsafe JavaScript functions. Use safe DOM manipulation methods, apply appropriate output encoding, validate user input where required, and implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) where possible.

title: Dangerous HTTP Methods Permitted
description: The web server permits HTTP methods beyond those required for normal application operation, such as PUT, DELETE, TRACE, or CONNECT. These methods may enable attackers to upload files to the server, delete content, or conduct cross-site tracing attacks.
impact: An attacker may be able to upload arbitrary files to the server using the PUT method, delete resources using the DELETE method, or retrieve HTTP header information including authentication cookies via the TRACE method. The specific impact depends on which methods are permitted and how the server handles them.
recommendations: Configure the web server to only allow the HTTP methods required by the application. Explicitly deny all other methods and return 405 Method Not Allowed. Disable the TRACE and TRACK methods to prevent cross-site tracing attacks. Review framework and server configuration to ensure method restrictions are applied consistently.

title: GraphQL Denial of Service via Query Depth or Complexity
description: The GraphQL API does not implement query depth limiting, complexity analysis, or field count restrictions. An attacker can craft deeply nested or highly complex queries that consume excessive server resources, potentially causing denial of service.
impact: An attacker may be able to craft GraphQL queries with excessive nesting or field expansion that cause the server to consume disproportionate resources in processing the request. This could degrade performance for all users of the application or result in complete service unavailability, depending on the available server resources and the degree of query complexity permitted.
recommendations: Implement query depth limiting to reject queries that exceed a maximum nesting level. Apply complexity analysis to assign costs to fields and mutations and reject queries that exceed a complexity budget. Consider implementing query timeouts and persisted queries to further limit the potential for abuse.

title: HTTP Verb Tampering
description: The application does not consistently enforce access controls or input validation across all HTTP methods. By switching from the expected HTTP method (e.g. GET) to an alternative method (e.g. POST, PUT, or arbitrary verbs), an attacker may be able to bypass security controls or trigger unintended application behaviour.
impact: An attacker may be able to bypass authentication checks, access controls, or input validation by using unexpected HTTP methods to access restricted functionality. In some cases, this can allow access to administrative functions, bypass CSRF protections, or trigger server-side behaviour that is not intended to be user-accessible.
recommendations: Implement access controls and input validation consistently for all HTTP methods. Configure the web server and application framework to only permit the HTTP methods required for each endpoint, and explicitly reject or return 405 Method Not Allowed for unexpected methods. Ensure security controls are applied at the framework level rather than in per-route handlers.

title: Host Header Injection
description: Host header injection occurs when an application trusts and uses the HTTP Host header without properly validating its value. An attacker can manipulate the Host header to influence application behaviour.
impact: An attacker may be able to exploit the application's trust in the Host header to poison password reset links delivered to users, cause the application to redirect or serve content from attacker-controlled domains, or influence web cache behaviour. The specific impact depends on how and where the application uses the Host header value.
recommendations: Validate the Host header against a list of trusted domains and avoid using user-controlled Host header values when generating URLs or security-sensitive content. Configure web servers and application frameworks to reject unexpected Host header values.

title: Insecure WebSocket Implementation
description: The application implements WebSocket connections without adequate security controls. This may include a failure to validate the Origin header, lack of authentication for WebSocket connections, missing input validation on WebSocket messages, or transmission of sensitive data without TLS.
impact: An attacker may be able to establish unauthorised WebSocket connections from a malicious website if the Origin header is not validated, hijack existing WebSocket sessions if authentication is not enforced, inject malicious messages if input validation is absent, or intercept messages transmitted without TLS. The specific impact depends on the application functionality exposed via the WebSocket connection.
recommendations: Validate the Origin header on WebSocket handshake requests against an allow-list of trusted origins. Enforce authentication for all WebSocket connections and revalidate session tokens at the handshake stage. Apply input validation and output encoding to all WebSocket message content, and ensure WebSocket connections use WSS (WebSocket Secure) over TLS.

title: JSONP Callback Data Leakage
description: The application exposes one or more JSONP (JSON with Padding) endpoints that return sensitive user-specific data wrapped in a user-controlled callback function name. JSONP was a legacy technique for cross-origin data sharing and does not enforce same-origin policy restrictions.
impact: An attacker may be able to include the JSONP endpoint as a script tag on a malicious website visited by an authenticated victim. The victim's browser will make a credentialled request to the endpoint and execute the response as JavaScript within the attacker's page context, allowing the attacker to capture and exfiltrate the victim's sensitive data returned by the endpoint.
recommendations: Replace JSONP endpoints with CORS-enabled JSON APIs that enforce strict origin validation. If JSONP must remain available, validate the callback parameter against an allow-list of known safe callback names and ensure that sensitive or authenticated data is not returned via JSONP endpoints. Implement authentication token validation that prevents cross-site use of credentialled responses.

title: Missing Anti-Automation Controls on Sensitive Functions
description: Sensitive application functions including account registration, OTP submission, voucher redemption, or content posting lack adequate anti-automation controls beyond basic rate limiting. The absence of device fingerprinting, behavioural analysis, or multi-factor friction means that automated tooling can interact with these endpoints with minimal friction.
impact: An attacker may be able to automate interactions with sensitive application functionality at scale, enabling high-volume account creation, credential stuffing, enumeration of valid discount codes or vouchers, automated content scraping, or resource exhaustion attacks. These attacks can cause financial loss, service degradation, or reputational damage without requiring any authentication.
recommendations: Implement layered anti-automation controls on sensitive endpoints including CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting, behavioural analysis, and progressive friction that increases with suspicious activity. Complement these controls with server-side rate limiting and anomaly detection, and implement alerting for unusual volumes of requests to high-risk endpoints.

title: No Account Lockout
description: Account lockout controls prevent repeated failed authentication attempts against user accounts. Without appropriate lockout or rate-limiting protections, an application may allow unlimited authentication attempts against valid accounts.
impact: An attacker may be able to make an unlimited number of authentication attempts against valid user accounts without being blocked or delayed. This facilitates automated brute force and credential stuffing attacks, increasing the likelihood of successfully compromising accounts that use weak or previously exposed passwords.
recommendations: Implement account lockout or rate-limiting controls after repeated failed authentication attempts. Consider using progressive delays, monitoring for suspicious authentication activity, and enforcing strong password policies to reduce the risk of credential compromise.

title: No Rate Limiting
description: Rate limiting controls restrict the number of requests or actions that can be performed within a defined period. Without appropriate rate limiting, applications may allow excessive requests to be made against sensitive functionality.
impact: An attacker may be able to submit an unlimited number of requests to sensitive application functions such as login pages, password reset flows, or one-time code verification endpoints. This could facilitate automated brute force and enumeration attacks against users or valid inputs at scale, without risk of detection or blocking by the application.
recommendations: Implement rate limiting controls on sensitive functionality such as authentication, password resets, account creation, and API endpoints. Apply appropriate thresholds, monitor for excessive request patterns, and consider implementing progressive delays or temporary blocking for repeated abuse.

title: Outdated Third-Party Libraries
description: Outdated third-party libraries occur when an application uses external dependencies that contain known vulnerabilities or no longer receive security updates. These libraries may introduce security weaknesses into the application.
impact: The use of third-party libraries with known vulnerabilities may expose the application to exploitation via publicly available proof-of-concept code or automated tooling. The specific impact depends on the nature of the vulnerabilities present in the affected dependencies, and could range from information disclosure to remote code execution depending on the library and version in use.
recommendations: Regularly review and update third-party dependencies to supported and secure versions. Remove unused libraries, monitor vulnerability disclosures for dependencies in use, and implement a software composition analysis (SCA) process where appropriate.

title: Prototype Pollution
description: Prototype pollution occurs when an application allows user-controlled input to modify properties of JavaScript object prototypes. An attacker can manipulate inherited properties that may influence application behaviour.
impact: An attacker may be able to inject properties into JavaScript object prototypes that are subsequently inherited by other objects across the application. Depending on how the polluted properties are used, this could lead to denial of service, bypass of security checks, or in server-side Node.js environments, potentially escalate to remote code execution.
recommendations: Avoid merging or copying untrusted objects directly into application objects. Validate and sanitise user input, use safe object handling methods, update vulnerable dependencies, and restrict access to prototype-modification functionality where possible.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) occurs when an application includes user-supplied input in an HTTP response without appropriate encoding, and the payload is reflected in the immediate response rather than being stored. An attacker must craft a malicious URL and deliver it to a victim to trigger execution.
impact: An attacker may be able to craft a malicious URL that, when clicked by a victim, causes a script to execute within the victim's browser session. This could be used to steal session cookies and hijack authenticated sessions, redirect the user to a malicious site, capture keystrokes, or perform actions within the application on behalf of the victim.
recommendations: Apply context-aware output encoding to all user-supplied data that is reflected in HTTP responses. Validate and sanitise input at the server side, implement a Content Security Policy, and use modern framework security features that provide automatic escaping for template rendering.

title: Sensitive Data Exposed in URL Parameters
description: The application transmits sensitive data including session tokens, API keys, or personal information as URL query parameters. URL parameters are logged in web server logs, browser history, and may be transmitted to third parties via the Referer header when the user navigates to an external link.
impact: Sensitive data transmitted in URL parameters may be recorded in server logs, proxy logs, browser history, and referrer logs of third-party sites. An attacker with access to any of these logs, or who can intercept the Referer header, may be able to retrieve session tokens or other sensitive data and use them to impersonate the victim or access protected resources.
recommendations: Avoid transmitting sensitive data as URL query parameters. Use POST request bodies or HTTP headers for sensitive values, and transmit session tokens exclusively via cookies with appropriate security flags. Ensure web server and proxy logs are configured to redact or mask sensitive parameters.

title: Session Fixation
description: Session fixation occurs when an application allows an attacker to set or influence a user's session identifier before authentication. If the session identifier is not regenerated after login, the attacker may be able to reuse the authenticated session.
impact: An attacker may be able to supply a known session identifier to a victim and, if the application does not regenerate the session token upon authentication, use that identifier to access the victim's authenticated session. This could allow the attacker to impersonate the victim and access any data or functionality available to that user's account.
recommendations: Regenerate session identifiers after authentication and privilege changes. Ensure session tokens are generated securely, invalidate old sessions when appropriate, and avoid accepting session identifiers from untrusted sources.

title: Weak Password Policy
description: Weak password policies occur when an application or system does not enforce sufficient password requirements, allowing users to create passwords that are easily guessed or susceptible to compromise.
impact: Users may be permitted to set passwords that are easily guessed or susceptible to offline cracking and credential stuffing attacks. If an attacker is able to compromise weak passwords, they could gain unauthorised access to affected accounts and any data or functionality accessible to those users, potentially including sensitive personal information or privileged application features.
recommendations:
Enforce a strong password policy that requires sufficiently complex and unique passwords. Implement protections against common and compromised passwords, enable multi-factor authentication where possible, and regularly review authentication controls. *Note:* NCSC now advises against complexity rules as they place a burden on users which often encourages them to reuse previous passwords with a minor alteration. For further advice see the article in the references.

title: Evil Twin Access Point Attack Feasibility
description:
Ruptura InfoSecurity confirmed that an evil twin attack was feasible against the wireless infrastructure in scope. An evil twin access point (AP) is a rogue wireless network that mimics a legitimate SSID and BSSID. Combined with a deauthentication attack (facilitated by the absence of 802.11w), clients can be forced to disconnect from the legitimate AP and reconnect to the attacker-controlled evil twin.

Once connected to the evil twin, all traffic from affected clients passes through the attacker's device, enabling credential interception for HTTP (cleartext) traffic and man-in-the-middle attacks against HTTPS traffic where certificate validation can be bypassed (e.g., applications ignoring certificate errors).

This finding was demonstrated in a controlled test environment using Hostapd-WPE for WPA2-Enterprise networks or a standard hostapd configuration for WPA2-PSK networks.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Successful evil twin attacks enable interception of all wireless traffic from affected clients, including authentication credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data. WPA2-Enterprise EAP-MD5 and PEAP configurations may leak domain credentials to a rogue RADIUS server.

**Business Impact:** Credential theft via evil twin attacks at corporate premises can result in Active Directory credential compromise, further enabling internal network access and lateral movement.
recommendations:
- Enable 802.11w (Protective Management Frames) to prevent deauthentication frame spoofing, which is required for effective evil twin forcing
- Migrate to WPA3 which includes PMF as mandatory
- For WPA2-Enterprise: validate the RADIUS server certificate in client supplicant profiles; configure devices to refuse connections to access points not presenting a known certificate
- Deploy a Wireless Intrusion Detection System (WIDS) to detect and alert on rogue APs matching corporate SSIDs
- Implement network access control (NAC) to ensure only managed devices join corporate networks

title: Insecure Guest Network Authentication (Pre-Shared Key)
description:
Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that the guest wireless network relied on a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) for authentication. Any user with knowledge of the PSK can authenticate to the network and browse anonymously without any audit trail linking activity to a specific individual. The PSK was also found to be of insufficient complexity and had not been rotated for an extended period.

Guest network access should follow a portal-based approval workflow (captive portal with registration), allowing the organisation to track users and their access duration, and to revoke access when necessary.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** A static PSK on a guest network with no audit trail means any past guest, current guest, or individual who learned the PSK can connect and browse the internet (and potentially probe internal network services) without accountability.

**Business Impact:** Anonymous network access makes it impossible to investigate security incidents originating from the guest network. Regulatory requirements for network monitoring may not be satisfied.
recommendations:
- Replace static PSK guest authentication with a captive portal requiring guest registration (name, email, mobile) with time-limited access credentials
- Implement a guest access management platform (e.g., Cisco ISE, Aruba ClearPass, or cloud-based guest portal) that generates per-user, time-limited credentials
- Enforce client isolation on the guest network to prevent guest-to-guest attacks
- Restrict guest network to internet-only access, blocking all internal RFC1918 addresses

title: Protective Management Frames (802.11w) Not Enabled
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that Protective Management Frames (PMF / IEEE 802.11w) was disabled across wireless networks in scope. 802.11w protects 802.11 management frames (including deauthentication and disassociation frames) from forgery. Without PMF, an attacker within wireless range can send forged deauthentication frames to disconnect any or all clients from the network, facilitating denial of service or forcing clients to reconnect through a rogue access point.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Without PMF, wireless deauthentication attacks can disconnect clients at will. This enables denial-of-service conditions for wireless users and, in combination with an evil twin access point, can force clients to connect to an attacker-controlled network, facilitating credential interception.

**Business Impact:** Targeted wireless denial of service can disrupt operations for wireless-dependent workloads. Forced reconnection to a rogue AP can enable credential theft.
recommendations:
- Enable 802.11w (Protective Management Frames) on all wireless networks; set to 'Required' for corporate networks and 'Optional' for guest networks (to accommodate legacy devices)
- WPA3 mandates PMF by default — migration to WPA3 addresses this control
- Implement rogue AP detection within the wireless infrastructure to detect evil twin attacks

title: WPA2-PSK Authentication Identified on Corporate Network
description:
Ruptura InfoSecurity identified that Wi-Fi networks in scope utilised WPA2 Pre-Shared Key (PSK) authentication, which requires a single shared password for network access. With PSK authentication, any device connecting to the network must present the same shared password. This password is stored on potentially hundreds of devices and may be written down or disclosed, increasing its likelihood of compromise.

Additionally, WPA2-PSK has inherent cryptographic weaknesses: an attacker within range can capture the 4-way handshake during client authentication and crack the PSK offline using tools such as Hashcat and a GPU. A cracked PSK provides full network access and the ability to decrypt historical traffic captured during the handshake.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** A cracked or disclosed PSK grants network access to any attacker within wireless range. Once on the network, the attacker can attempt lateral movement to internal systems, perform man-in-the-middle attacks against other clients, and access internal services not exposed externally.

**Business Impact:** WPA2-PSK is widely regarded as unsuitable for corporate environments. Its use may fail PCI-DSS wireless security requirements and represent a systemic weakness in the network security posture.
recommendations:
- Migrate all corporate wireless networks from WPA2-PSK to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X/EAP)
- WPA2-Enterprise authenticates individual users or devices using unique credentials (certificates or username/password), eliminating the shared PSK weakness
- Deploy a RADIUS server (Microsoft NPS, FreeRADIUS, or cloud-based) to support 802.1X authentication
- As an interim measure, implement MAC address filtering and ensure the PSK is a long, random string not derived from organisation information
- Rotate the PSK immediately upon any suspected disclosure

title: Inadequate Wireless Client Isolation
description: Ruptura InfoSecurity identified wireless networks that did not enforce client isolation. Client isolation (also known as AP isolation or wireless isolation) prevents devices connected to the same wireless network from communicating directly with each other at the network level. Without isolation, a device connected to the wireless network can directly reach other connected clients, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks, traffic sniffing, and lateral movement between guest or untrusted devices.
impact:
**Technical Impact:** Without client isolation on networks with untrusted users (guest networks, public Wi-Fi, BYOD networks), a connected attacker can perform ARP spoofing to position themselves as a man-in-the-middle between victims and the gateway, sniff all broadcast traffic, and probe other connected devices for vulnerabilities.

**Business Impact:** Guest or untrusted devices sharing a network without isolation represent a lateral movement risk. Visitors or compromised guest devices could attack other guests or attempt to pivot toward internal network segments.
recommendations:
- Enable client/AP isolation on all guest networks and networks hosting untrusted devices
- Ensure isolation is enforced at both the access point and controller level
- Implement network segmentation to separate guest, corporate, and IoT wireless networks into isolated VLANs
- Restrict guest network access to internet-only, blocking all RFC1918 internal IP access
